title: Supervised aerobic and resistance training and glycaemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes: a randomised controlled trial
abstract: Background: Exercise is recommended in type 2 diabetes but the relative contribution of supervised training remains debated. Methods: We randomised 214 adults aged 35-70 with established type 2 diabetes to a 24-week supervised programme of combined aerobic and resistance training (three sessions per week) or to usual care. The primary outcome was change in HbA1c at 24 weeks. Results: Mean HbA1c fell by 0.74 percentage points in the intervention arm versus 0.11 in controls (between-group difference -0.63, 95% CI -0.85 to -0.41, p<0.001). Conclusions: Structured supervised exercise produced a clinically meaningful reduction in HbA1c.

title: Effects of a home-based walking programme on quality of life in older adults with type 2 diabetes
abstract: Objective: To evaluate whether an unsupervised home walking programme improves health-related quality of life. Design: Randomised controlled trial with 180 participants aged 60 and over with type 2 diabetes. Intervention: Twelve weeks of self-directed walking with a pedometer and monthly telephone support. Outcomes: The primary outcome was the SF-36 physical component score. Secondary outcomes included six-minute walk distance and self-reported adherence. Results: Quality of life improved modestly in the intervention arm. Glycaemic markers were not assessed in this trial.

title: Exercise interventions in type 2 diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 47 randomised trials
abstract: We searched MEDLINE, Embase and CENTRAL to June 2024 for randomised trials of exercise interventions in adults with type 2 diabetes reporting HbA1c. Forty-seven trials (n=4,912) met inclusion criteria. Pooled analysis showed a mean reduction in HbA1c of 0.57 percentage points (95% CI -0.71 to -0.43) favouring exercise. Heterogeneity was substantial. We conclude that exercise reduces HbA1c, with supervised programmes showing larger effects than unsupervised ones.

title: Treadmill training attenuates hyperglycaemia in a db/db mouse model of type 2 diabetes
abstract: Purpose: To characterise the metabolic response to endurance training in a rodent model. Methods: Male db/db mice were assigned to eight weeks of treadmill running or sedentary control. Fasting glucose, glycated haemoglobin and skeletal muscle GLUT4 expression were measured. Results: Trained animals showed lower fasting glucose and increased GLUT4 protein. Conclusions: Endurance training improves glycaemic parameters in this model, supporting further translational investigation.

title: Structured resistance training in adults with type 2 diabetes: a randomised trial of glycaemic and body composition outcomes
abstract: Aims: To determine the effect of a supervised progressive resistance training programme on glycaemic control. Methods: Ninety-six adults (mean age 58) with type 2 diabetes of at least one year's duration were randomised to 16 weeks of supervised resistance training three times weekly or to a stretching control. HbA1c, fasting insulin and DXA-measured lean mass were assessed at baseline and 16 weeks. Results: HbA1c decreased by 0.51 percentage points in the training group versus 0.06 in controls (p=0.003). Lean mass increased by 1.4 kg.

title: Continuous glucose monitoring adherence in adolescents with type 1 diabetes: a prospective cohort study
abstract: Background: Continuous glucose monitoring improves outcomes but adherence in adolescence is poor. Methods: We followed 240 adolescents aged 12-18 with type 1 diabetes for twelve months, recording sensor wear time and HbA1c. Results: Median wear time was 62%. Higher wear time was associated with lower HbA1c. Conclusions: Interventions to sustain sensor use in adolescents with type 1 diabetes are needed.

title: Protocol for a randomised trial of high-intensity interval training versus moderate continuous training in type 2 diabetes (the HIIT-T2D study)
abstract: Introduction: Whether high-intensity interval training confers greater glycaemic benefit than moderate continuous exercise in type 2 diabetes is unresolved. Methods and analysis: We will randomise 300 adults with type 2 diabetes to 12 weeks of supervised HIIT or moderate continuous training. The primary outcome is change in HbA1c. Ethics and dissemination: The study has ethical approval and results will be published in a peer-reviewed journal. Trial registration: NCT05xxxxxx.

title: Supervised circuit training improves glycaemic control in a randomised trial of adults with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes
abstract: We randomised 130 adults with type 2 diabetes and baseline HbA1c above 8.0% to a 20-week supervised circuit training intervention or to standard dietary advice. Sessions were delivered three times weekly by an exercise physiologist. The primary endpoint was HbA1c at 20 weeks, analysed by intention to treat. Mean HbA1c fell from 8.6% to 7.7% in the intervention group and from 8.5% to 8.3% in controls. Adverse events were infrequent and minor.

title: Dietary fibre supplementation and glycaemic outcomes in adults with type 2 diabetes: a randomised crossover trial
abstract: Objective: To assess whether 12 weeks of psyllium supplementation improves glycaemic control. Design: Randomised crossover trial in 64 adults with type 2 diabetes. Intervention: 10 g psyllium daily versus placebo, with a four-week washout. Outcomes: HbA1c, fasting glucose and postprandial glucose excursion. Results: HbA1c fell by 0.28 percentage points on psyllium relative to placebo (p=0.04). No exercise component was included.

title: Yoga and glycaemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes: a randomised controlled trial of a supervised twelve-week programme
abstract: Background: Mind-body exercise is increasingly offered in diabetes services but evidence is mixed. Methods: 148 adults with type 2 diabetes were randomised to a supervised twelve-week yoga programme (three sessions weekly, instructor-led) or a waitlist control. The primary outcome was HbA1c at twelve weeks; secondary outcomes included fasting glucose, blood pressure and perceived stress. Results: HbA1c declined by 0.42 percentage points in the yoga arm versus 0.09 in controls (p=0.01).
